<reason>A very close, high-quality debate. CON was better grounded (DC/Maine server opposition, Danny Meyer's reversal, the legal tip top-up floor) and landed the sharpest single rebuttal round, but CON built its case on an abolition reading the motion does not actually require: the proposition is about not relying on tips as the compensation base, not banning voluntary gratuities. PRO exploited this progressively, stacking CON's concessions (print the charge, raise the floor, pool with the kitchen, boss already controls sections) into a world where the tip is a gift atop a wage funded by honest prices — which is the motion as written. CON's closing "replace" dichotomy was a strong final move, but its horns ("nothing replaced" vs "takes from workers") are not exhaustive: a living wage funded by disclosed prices with optional gratuities on top does replace tipping-based compensation without eliminating the worker's upside. PRO also turned the owner-discretion attack (tip pooling relies on the same owner) and kept the variance/lottery-winners frame live. Costs for PRO: three clipped speeches and a late statute commitment that CON fairly flagged. Costs for CON: the nurses answer was circular and the "one boss vs 500 strangers" point was neutralized by CON's own admission that managers already control sections and hours. Razor-thin edge to PRO.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Rebuttal 2 concession-stack ([A4.5]) turning CON's own ledger — legible menu, raised floor, kitchen pooling, existing manager control — into the PRO world, answered by CON's "replace is the verb" closing; PRO's response that "rely" and "higher base pay" are in the motion held up slightly better. Honorable mention to CON's Rebuttal 1 "Pick one" and the tip top-up floor point, which forced PRO onto the defensive.</best_rebuttal>
